**ABSTRACT**

Current food systems rely on a limited number of cultivated species, while a wide diversity of orphan crops with high nutritional, adaptive, and cultural potential remains underutilized. This situation poses a challenge to food security, climate change adaptation, and the sustainability of agricultural systems, particularly in megadiverse countries such as Peru, where the current state of scientific research and conservation of these plant genetic resources remains poorly documented. The present study aimed to characterize scientific production and assess the current status of germplasm banks for orphan crops in Peru using a mixed-methods approach that integrated a bibliometric analysis of 157 publications indexed in Scopus with a national survey conducted among 11 institutions responsible for the conservation of plant genetic resources. Eleven priority orphan crops were identified, and research trends, collaboration networks, thematic evolution, and the conceptual structure of the scientific literature were analyzed. Likewise, 16,904 accessions conserved in germplasm banks distributed across eight departments of the country were characterized. Quinoa (*Chenopodium quinoa*) showed the highest scientific output (47 keyword occurrences) and the largest representation in conserved collections (4,344 accessions), followed by *Amaranthus caudatus* (16 occurrences; 3,603 accessions) and *Lupinus mutabilis* (3,344 accessions). Thematic evolution revealed a transition from studies focused on morphological characterization and germplasm conservation toward research addressing genetic diversity, plant breeding, and the application of molecular tools. Although Peru possesses a remarkable diversity of plant genetic resources conserved *ex situ*, institutional disparities were identified in infrastructure, documentation, regeneration, and collection management. These findings provide a baseline for strengthening national strategies for the conservation, research, and sustainable use of orphan crops as strategic resources for enhancing the resilience of food systems.

**Keywords:** agrobiodiversity; bibliometric analysis; conservation; germplasm; plant genetic resources. 


<div style='margin-top: 3em;'></div>

# **INTRODUCTION**

Contemporary agricultural systems face challenges arising from population growth, natural resource degradation, biodiversity loss, and the effects of climate change on food production [(Morton, 2007; Reidsma et al., 2010; Muluneh, 2021\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?7b8bn9). These conditions increase the vulnerability of production systems and compromise their capacity to meet the future demand for nutritious and accessible food [(Reidsma et al., 2010; Mogollón et al., 2026\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?ddUTVW). Enhancing agrobiodiversity has been recognized as a strategy to strengthen agroecosystem resilience, reduce dependence on a limited number of cultivated species, and promote more sustainable production systems [(Renard & Tilman, 2019; Hiywotu et al., 2026\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?UTsTgM). Therefore, harnessing the genetic diversity available in cultivated plants and their wild relatives constitutes an essential component for addressing challenges related to food security and adapting agriculture to changing environmental conditions. .

Orphan crops, also referred to as neglected and underutilized species (NUS) [(Hunter et al., 2019\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?TdD0iB), are plant species that, following prolonged processes of domestication and farmer-driven selection in their regions of origin or naturalization, have remained largely overlooked by scientific research, plant breeding, and agricultural development policies despite their recognized food, nutritional, economic, and cultural value [(Dawson et al., 2007; Padulosi et al., 2014; Talabi et al., 2022; MacNish et al., 2025\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?9l79MY). The term “orphan” refers to the limited attention these species have received from scientific research, breeding programs, and agricultural development policies rather than to their agronomic importance. These species constitute fundamental resources for local communities because of their high genetic diversity, adaptation to marginal environments, and resilience to biotic and abiotic stresses. Moreover, their status is context-dependent, as a crop may be widely cultivated and commercialized in one region while remaining underutilized or insufficiently studied in another [(Tadele & Bartels, 2019; Talabi et al., 2022\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?SB2JVx)

The growing recognition of the agronomic, nutritional, and environmental characteristics of these crops has promoted their incorporation into international initiatives aimed at diversifying agricultural production and strengthening the resilience of food systems [(Toledo & Burlingame, 2006; Ruiz et al., 2014; Chivenge et al., 2015; Vera et al., 2025\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?T7H5O6). Several studies have documented that these crops possess the capacity to adapt to adverse environmental conditions, tolerate biotic and abiotic stresses, and maintain cultural and historical significance for numerous rural communities [(Malice et al., 2010; Coloma et al., 2022; Lozano-Isla et al., 2023; Baldera-Chapoñan et al., 2025b; Ortega-Quispe et al., 2026\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?GgDTGp), representing an important source of genetic diversity that could be harnessed to expand the options available to address the challenges facing contemporary agriculture.

Peru is recognized as a center of origin and diversification for numerous cultivated species, harboring substantial diversity of plant genetic resources associated with different ecological regions and traditional production systems [(Velásquez-Milla et al., 2011; Jacobsen et al., 2015; Maxted & Vincent, 2021\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Xk7ElE). This diversity has been maintained through historical processes of selection and management developed by local communities, contributing to the conservation of a broad genetic pool [(Velásquez-Milla et al., 2011\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?QL9VdM). Among the species of interest are arracacha (*Arracacia xanthorrhiza*), cañihua (*Chenopodium pallidicaule*), chia (*Salvia hispanica*), kiwicha (*Amaranthus caudatus*), maca (*Lepidium meyenii*), mashua (*Tropaeolum tuberosum*), oca (*Oxalis tuberosa*), olluco (*Ullucus tuberosus*), quinoa (*Chenopodium quinoa* Willd.), tarwi (*Lupinus mutabilis*), and yacón (*Smallanthus sonchifolius*), which represent an important fraction of Andean agrobiodiversity and have attracted increasing interest because of their nutritional properties, adaptation to diverse environments, and potential to contribute to the diversification of agricultural systems [(Ruiz et al., 2014; Repo-Carrasco-Valencia et al., 2022; Luera-Quiñones et al., 2025\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?yokXFQ). However, the level of knowledge and utilization of these resources remains variable among species, highlighting the need to consolidate information that can guide research and conservation efforts. 

The conservation of plant genetic resources constitutes a fundamental strategy for safeguarding the genetic diversity required for the development of breeding programs, scientific research, and the adaptation of crops to new environmental conditions [(Esquinas-Alcázar, 2005; Dempewolf et al., 2014; Priyanka et al., 2021\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?jyGfth). Among the different strategies available, *ex situ* conservation through germplasm banks plays a central role by enabling the collection, characterization, documentation, regeneration, and maintenance of accessions representative of existing variability. These banks serve as repositories of genetic resources and provide biological material for research, education, and agricultural development activities [(Priyanka et al., 2021\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?LDhmcU). Strengthening the technical and institutional capacities dedicated to the management of these collections is essential to ensure the future availability of strategic genetic resources. 

At the international level, specific programs have been established for the conservation and sustainable use of plant genetic resources of agronomic importance [(Khoury et al., 2010; Dempewolf et al., 2014; Byrne et al., 2018\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?74YMD8). However, the effectiveness of germplasm banks depends on factors such as the availability of adequate infrastructure, the implementation of standardized conservation protocols, the existence of efficient documentation systems, and access to trained human resources [(Priyanka et al., 2021\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?DALnRx). In the absence of these conditions, collections may face risks associated with the loss of viability of conserved material, unnecessary duplication of efforts, or limited accessibility to the information generated. Therefore, periodic assessments of the status of germplasm banks constitute necessary tools for identifying strengths, limitations, and priority intervention needs. 

In Peru, various public and private institutions, universities, and research centers conduct activities related to the conservation of plant genetic resources of agricultural importance. However, information on collections associated with orphan crops remains scattered and, in many cases, has not been systematized or disseminated through scientific publications. Similarly, limited knowledge exists regarding the conditions under which germplasm conservation is carried out, including aspects related to available infrastructure, management procedures, record-keeping systems, and institutional capacities to ensure the sustainability of collections. This situation hinders the development of a comprehensive understanding of the current status of *ex situ* conservation of these genetic resources in the country. 

Despite the growing recognition of the potential of orphan crops to contribute to agricultural diversification, food security, and the adaptation of production systems to climate change scenarios [(Malice et al., 2010; Coloma et al., 2022; Baldera-Chapoñan et al., 2025; Ortega-Quispe et al., 2026\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?7n6W8l), limitations persist regarding the availability and systematization of information on the genetic resources associated with these species in Peru. Existing studies have focused primarily on the agronomic or nutritional characterization of specific crops, whereas research aimed at comprehensively assessing the status of germplasm banks responsible for their conservation remains scarce. Information concerning collection size, conservation methods, available documentation systems, and institutional capacities for germplasm management remains scattered or has not been reported in the scientific literature. This situation hinders the identification of gaps in conservation programs and limits the development of evidence-based national strategies to strengthen the management of plant genetic resources. 

Therefore, the present study aimed to: (i) conduct a bibliographic analysis to identify and characterize orphan crops reported in Peru; (ii) assess the current status of germplasm banks involved in the conservation of these crops through surveys administered to the responsible institutions; and (iii) diagnose the conservation and management conditions of these germplasm banks, with the aim of generating information to support the development of strategies for strengthening the conservation of plant genetic resources of current and potential importance to Peruvian agriculture.

# **MATERIALS AND METHODS**

This study employed a mixed-methods, exploratory-descriptive approach structured into two stages. The first stage consisted of a bibliometric analysis of scientific production related to orphan crops of relevance to Peruvian agriculture, allowing the current state of research and the main themes addressed regarding the conservation and utilization of these plant genetic resources to be identified. The second stage involved the development of a national inventory and an assessment of the status of germplasm banks and conservation strategies associated with these crops through surveys administered to researchers and a review of available institutional catalogs and inventories.  

## ***Extraction and Processing of Bibliometric Data*** 

The Scopus database was selected as the bibliographic information source because of its extensive coverage of peer-reviewed scientific literature, standardized bibliographic records, and frequent use in bibliometric studies and scientific trend analyses [(Baas et al., 2020; Donthu et al., 2021\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?J6cLnC). The systematic search was conducted on July 6, 2026, at 11:00 UTC−5, using search equations specific to each crop and the TITLE-ABS-KEY field, which retrieves terms appearing in titles, abstracts, and keywords. The search strategies consisted of the scientific name of each species combined with the term “germplasm” (@tbl-ecu), with the aim of identifying studies related to the evaluation, conservation, and utilization of genetic resources in Andean crops and underutilized species. 

The initial search retrieved 222 scientific records corresponding to the eleven species evaluated. Subsequently, subject-area filters were applied through the Scopus results interface, restricting the results to Agricultural and Biological Sciences and Biochemistry, Genetics and Molecular Biology, which reduced the dataset to 206 documents. Documents classified as reviews were excluded because the analysis focused exclusively on original research and experimental studies, resulting in a total of 201 records for the eligibility assessment stage through title and abstract screening. 

### ***Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria*** 

Following the application of bibliographic filters in the Scopus database, titles and abstracts were screened to determine study eligibility. Studies that met the following criteria were included: 

1. Studies conducted on Andean crops and underutilized species of importance for food security, including *Amaranthus caudatus*, *Arracacia xanthorrhiza*, *Chenopodium pallidicaule*, *Chenopodium quinoa*, *Lepidium meyenii*, *Lupinus mutabilis*, *Oxalis tuberosa*, *Salvia hispanica*, *Smallanthus sonchifolius*, *Tropaeolum tuberosum*, and *Ullucus tuberosus*.  
2. Studies that evaluated germplasm collections, accessions, landraces, cultivars, or genetic materials.  
3. Studies focused on the phenotypic, morphological, agronomic, physiological, biochemical, or molecular characterization of genetic diversity.  
4. Studies reporting evaluation methodologies, descriptors used, statistical analyses, or molecular tools employed for the characterization, conservation, or utilization of genetic variability.

Subsequently, at 16:45 UTC−5 on the same day, 160 records meeting the established eligibility criteria were obtained. These records were exported from Scopus in comma-separated values (.csv) format, including bibliographic information, citation data, abstracts, keywords, institutional affiliations, and funding details. The database was then cleaned by identifying duplicate records using the Digital Object Identifier (DOI), resulting in the removal of three duplicate documents (@fig-prisma). The final database comprised 157 scientific records, which were used for the bibliometric analysis of germplasm conservation, characterization, and utilization in Andean crops and underutilized species [(Page et al., 2021; Sarkis-Onofre et al., 2021\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?lDcUwK).

## ***Germplasm Bank Inventory*** 

A structured questionnaire was developed using the Google Forms platform to collect information on the status of germplasm banks for orphan crops in Peru (Supplementary Material 1). The instrument consisted of closed-ended and multiple-choice questions addressing the participating institution, conserved species, number of accessions, conservation methods and status, types of characterization performed, availability of documented information, and the main limitations affecting collection management. 

The questionnaire was distributed by email to 22 researchers responsible for germplasm banks affiliated with universities, research institutes, and public entities involved in the conservation of plant genetic resources (Supplementary Material 2). Responses were obtained from 10 participants who were engaged in activities related to the conservation, characterization, or management of orphan crop germplasm. The species considered were *Amaranthus caudatus*, *Arracacia xanthorrhiza*, *Chenopodium pallidicaule*, *Chenopodium quinoa*, *Lepidium meyenii*, *Lupinus mutabilis*, *Oxalis tuberosa*, *Salvia hispanica*, *Smallanthus sonchifolius*, *Tropaeolum tuberosum*, and *Ullucus tuberosus*. The information collected was complemented with data obtained from the Germplasm Bank of the National Institute for Agrarian Innovation (SIRGE; [https://sirge.inia.gob.pe/index](https://sirge.inia.gob.pe/index)) [(INIA 2026\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?CaPC53), from which records related to the study species were extracted, including information on conserved collections and available accessions. The recorded information was exported from Google Forms to a spreadsheet, where record consistency was assessed, variables were standardized, and a database was organized for subsequent data analysis.

## ***Statistical analysis*** 

The bibliometric analysis was conducted using the Bibliometrix v5.4.1 package [(Aria & Cuccurullo, 2016\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?zeyJ6j) executed in R v6.4.1 [(R Core Team, 2026\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?RjizRw) through its Biblioshiny graphical interface. This tool was used to process the main data workflow and calculate scientific productivity and impact indicators. The temporal trends in publications and citations were modeled using second-order polynomial regression, with goodness of fit assessed using the coefficient of determination (R²), complemented by Pearson’s correlation coefficient between the annual number of documents and citations. Biblioshiny was used to perform keyword analysis to generate the term-frequency word cloud, thematic trend map, longitudinal thematic evolution diagram divided into four time periods, and thematic map based on centrality and density indicators to classify concepts into basic, motor, niche, and emerging or declining themes. VOSviewer v1.6.21 [(van Eck & Waltman, 2010\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?sl4bTh) was specifically used to construct, visualize, and map the contribution and international collaboration networks among countries based on co-authorship, applying a minimum threshold of five interactions per node. 

# **RESULTS AND DISCUSSION**

The consolidation of resilient food systems requires plant genetic resources to be transformed into strategic infrastructure for the agriculture of the future. In Peru, orphan crops represent a key genetic resource for addressing climate change, while their digital and advanced characterization can transform agrobiodiversity into actionable knowledge for plant breeding. Germplasm banks should evolve from conservation repositories into dynamic centers for characterization, bioprospecting, and the exchange of data and genetic material. This transformation would enable the establishment of a national and international scientific network capable of harnessing Peru’s genetic diversity and accelerating the development of solutions for food security. 

## ***The Landscape of Orphan Crops***

### ***Analysis of Global Scientific Production***   

The analysis of annual scientific production, based on the aggregation of 157 records indexed in Scopus, revealed a temporal pattern characterized by an initial phase of low productivity, followed by a progressive increase in the number of publications and variable citation dynamics (@fig-produ-cientifica). During the period from 1989 to the late 1990s, scientific production remained low, ranging from one to two publications per year, whereas citation counts were relatively high in specific years, such as 1989 and 1998, indicating the presence of contributions with substantial cumulative impact. From the early 2000s onward, a gradual expansion in scientific production was observed, reaching three to six publications annually during the 2000s, accompanied by an increase in citations, with a pronounced peak in 2007 associated with highly influential documents in the field. 

Since 2018, a sustained intensification in scientific production was recorded, with values exceeding eight publications per year and a maximum of nearly twenty documents in 2022, representing the highest point in the series analyzed. Citation counts showed a fluctuating pattern, with notable peaks in 2012 and 2022, whereas a relative decline was observed in the most recent years, attributable to the temporal lag between document publication and citation accumulation. These results confirm a recent expansion of scientific activity and an increase in the impact of the field analyzed. 

### ***Scientific Production and Collaboration Networks*** 

The international co-authorship network (≥5 collaborations; @fig-red-colaboracion) comprised 16 countries organized into five collaboration clusters. Only countries with at least five international collaborations were included in the analysis. Cluster 1 (red) consisted of the United States, Peru, Colombia, Bolivia, Belgium, and Denmark. Cluster 2 (green) included India, Germany, Italy, and Chile. Cluster 3 (blue) comprised China and Argentina. Cluster 4 (purple) included Spain and Mexico, whereas Cluster 5 (yellow) consisted of Ecuador and the Netherlands. The distribution of nodes showed extensive connectivity among the clusters, with multiple links between countries belonging to different collaboration groups. This structure indicates the formation of an international scientific network focused on the study of native and underutilized crops, in which cooperation between countries with abundant plant genetic resources and those with greater technological capacity facilitates knowledge generation on the conservation, characterization, and utilization of agricultural diversity. 

The United States and Peru exhibited the largest nodes and the highest number of links within the network, followed by Colombia, Spain, India, and Germany. Peru’s central position within the network is associated with its importance as a center of origin and diversification of cultivated species, harboring extensive genetic variability of Andean crops such as *Amaranthus caudatus, Chenopodium pallidicaule, Chenopodium quinoa, Lepidium meyenii, Lupinus mutabilis, Oxalis tuberosa, Smallanthus sonchifolius, Tropaeolum tuberosum, and Ullucus tuberosus* (@fig-red-colaboracion). This diversity has been conserved through traditional management and selection practices carried out by Andean communities, constituting an important source of genetic resources for research on environmental adaptation, nutritional quality, and plant breeding [(Tapia & Fries, 2007; Velásquez-Milla et al., 2011; Graddy, 2014; Baldera-Chapoñan et al., 2025\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Uxto6t).

The United States established direct collaborations with Peru, Colombia, Bolivia, Belgium, Germany, and Spain, whereas Peru recorded links with the United States, Colombia, Bolivia, Belgium, Denmark, and Ecuador (@fig-red-colaboracion). The strong connection between the two countries reflects the complementarity between the availability of native germplasm and scientific capacity for conducting advanced studies in genetics, biotechnology, nutritional analysis, and agronomic evaluation. Andean crops have gained increasing international relevance because of their capacity to adapt to restrictive environmental conditions and their potential to contribute to the diversification of food systems under scenarios associated with climate change and food security [(Baldera-Chapoñan et al., 2025; Chalampuente-Flores et al., 2023; Cui et al., 2024; Fernández-Poquioma et al., 2026; Gómez & Colín, 2008; Manzelli et al., 2004; Vleugels et al., 2024\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?xC4FPo) 

The participation of European countries such as Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Italy, Spain, and the Netherlands within the network indicates growing interest in crops outside conventional agricultural systems. In these countries, research on quinoa, amaranth, tarwi, and other Andean crops has been associated with the identification of functional properties, nutritional composition, bioactive metabolites, and production alternatives for specialized markets [(Bellucci et al., 2021; Bonnave et al., 2014, 2016; Vleugels et al., 2024\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?wFz19m). The incorporation of advanced analytical tools and multidisciplinary approaches has broadened the understanding of the biological and agronomic value of these resources, facilitating their integration into international research and conservation programs. 

Spain presented connections with the United States, Germany, Mexico, Colombia, and Ecuador, whereas Germany was linked to India, Italy, Chile, the United States, and Spain, demonstrating the participation of countries with established capacities in genetic, technological, and food research (@fig-red-colaboracion). The presence of India and China within the network reflects growing international interest in alternative crops with relevant nutritional characteristics and the capacity to adapt to diverse environmental conditions, considering these countries’ experience in the conservation and utilization of plant genetic resources. Ecuador maintained links with Peru, Spain, Denmark, and the Netherlands, whereas China and Argentina formed an independent cluster with a connection between the two countries, and Mexico showed a primarily strong relationship with Spain. This structure reflects the expansion of research on Andean crops and underutilized species through regional and international collaboration networks; however, scientific production remains concentrated on species with greater global recognition, such as quinoa, while other native crops, including mashua, ulluco, arracacha, maca, and yacon, have a lower presence in the scientific literature despite their agricultural, ecological, and nutritional importance.  

The corresponding authors’ single-country publications (SCP) and multiple-country publications (MCP) showed differences among the main producing countries (@fig-dis-pais). Peru recorded the highest number of documents, with a predominance of single-country publications, followed by the United States (15), where internationally collaborative publications represented a substantial proportion of the scientific output. Colombia and India each accounted for 11 documents, with a greater contribution from SCP. China reached 10 publications, whereas Chile recorded nine documents with a relatively balanced distribution between SCP and MCP. Mexico ranked next with seven publications, followed by Argentina with six, and Germany and Italy with five documents each. Belgium and Bolivia presented publications under both collaboration modalities. Denmark, the Czech Republic, and Ecuador were represented exclusively by multiple-country publications, whereas Turkey and Egypt recorded only single-country publications (@fig-dis-pais). 

The author co-authorship network (≥3 collaborations; @fig-coautoria) identified a cluster comprising Maughan P. J., Jellen E. N., Stevens M. R., Fairbanks D. J., Coleman C. E., and Bonifacio A., whose studies focused on the characterization and conservation of plant genetic resources of Andean crops. Publications produced by this group addressed the genetic diversity of *Chenopodium quinoa* Willd., *Chenopodium pallidicaule*, and *Amaranthus caudatus* germplasm through the use of SSR and SNP molecular markers, the development of genetic maps, genome sequencing, and the evaluation of populations for plant breeding [(Fairbanks et al., 1990; Vargas et al., 2011; Jimenez et al., 2013; Bonnave et al., 2014, 2016; Mangelson et al., 2019; Lozano-Isla et al., 2023\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?OFOGLg). The cluster’s studies also included research on downy mildew resistance, seed protein characterization, and salinity stress responses in tolerant quinoa accessions [(Benlhabib et al., 2016; Cueva-Flores et al., 2024\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Be9Vsy). The high frequency of collaboration among these authors reflects a research line focused on the study of genetic diversity and the utilization of plant genetic resources in orphan crops (@fig-coautoria). 

### ***Citation analysis***

### ***Keyword Analysis*** 

To analyze the conceptual structure of research on genetic resources and the breeding of Andean crops, author keywords were used to identify the most frequently occurring terms, recognize the main thematic trends, and assess the evolution of research lines. 

The keyword cloud (@fig-plabras-claves) revealed the predominance of terms related to germplasm (53 occurrences), *Chenopodium quinoa* (47), genetic diversity (35), and plant breeding (18), highlighting the importance of the conservation, characterization, and utilization of genetic resources in Andean crops. The high frequency of the term germplasm reflects the fundamental role of plant genetic resource collections as sources of variability for studies of genetic diversity, genotype selection, and the development of improved materials [(Barba-Espin & Acosta-Motos, 2022; Salgotra & Chauhan, 2023\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?GayqsR). he presence of terms such as genetic marker (14), population structure (11), genetic variability (10), and molecular markers (6) indicates the incorporation of genomic tools for assessing genetic relationships and identifying diversity patterns in plant populations. Likewise, the frequency of *Amaranthus caudatus* (16), *Amaranthus hypochondriacus* (6), *Oxalis tuberosa* (6), and *Solanum tuberosum* (5) reflects scientific interest in Andean species of agricultural importance and potential for production diversification. The occurrence of terms such as morphology, genotype, protein, grain yield, and multivariate analysis indicates the integration of phenotypic evaluations and statistical tools for the characterization of accessions and the identification of materials with favorable agronomic attributes. 

The thematic trend analysis revealed the temporal evolution of keywords associated with this research field, highlighting a clear transition from morphological and regional studies toward molecular approaches and advanced plant breeding. The initial stages focused on basic geographical and taxonomic identification, with terms such as *Chenopodium*, Peru, *Amaranthus cruentus*, Bolivia, *Amaranthus hypochondriacus*, and South America reaching their highest frequency between 2005 and 2007 (@fig-evo-temporal). This trend reflects the initial interest in documenting the biological diversity and distribution of Andean species, constituting a fundamental stage for establishing reference collections and understanding the diversity available within plant genetic resources [(Bazile et al., 2016\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?jLJTQz). Subsequently, scientific interest shifted toward basic phenotypic, morphological, and agronomic characterization through concepts such as *Oxalis tuberosa*, morphology, phenotype, and cultivar, which consolidated their presence toward the end of the 2000s, demonstrating the importance of observable traits as a basis for the preliminary classification and selection of genetic materials [(Akter et al., 2026; Baldera-Chapoñan et al., 2025; Chalampuente-Flores et al., 2023; Manzelli et al., 2004; Ortega-Quispe et al., 2026; Snowball et al., 2022\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?MPg0q4)

The period from 2010 to 2015 marked the phase of greatest thematic volume and consolidation, led by research on genetic resources and key Andean crops, with *germplasm* showing the highest cumulative frequency, followed by *Chenopodium quinoa*, *genetic diversity*, the Andes, *Amaranthus caudatus*, wild populations, phylogeny, and genetic variability. This pattern indicates a shift toward the conservation, evaluation, and utilization of genetic diversity as a strategy to strengthen plant breeding programs, particularly for species adapted to marginal environments and of importance for food security (@fig-evo-temporal). From 2016 onward, the research trend adopted a more analytical profile through the use of molecular, bioinformatic, and statistical tools represented by terms such as genotype, molecular analysis, multivariate analysis, and population structure, reflecting the incorporation of genomic technologies to characterize the genetic organization of populations and facilitate marker-assisted selection [(Barut et al., 2020; Bhargava, Shukla, Rajan, et al., 2007; Costa Tártara et al., 2012; Craine & Murphy, 2020; De la Cruz et al., 2025; Fernández-Poquioma et al., 2026\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Sg5zMA). Recent studies have focused directly on yield optimization and applied biotechnology, positioning terms such as genetic structure, genetics, plant breeding, grain yield, yield, breeding, and molecular markers as current and emerging research fronts, demonstrating an increasing integration of genomic information with phenotypic evaluation for the development of superior cultivars [(Rasheed et al., 2017\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?4KZUCS).

The longitudinal thematic evolution map tracks the trajectory, branching, and consolidation of the cognitive structure of research across four specific periods between 1989 and 2026 (@fig-evo-tematica). The initial period (1989-2010) established the scientific foundation through phenotypic and taxonomic characterization, represented by the nodes *genetic variability*, *germplasm*, *phenotype*, *Chenopodium quinoa*, *dicotyledon*, and *Amaranthus caudatus*, reflecting interest in describing biological diversity, establishing taxonomic relationships, and generating a basis for the conservation of plant genetic resources [(Risi & Galwey, 1989; Fairbanks et al., 1990; Ortiz et al., 1998; Trognitz et al., 1998; Sun et al., 1999\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?w6mQcJ). This pattern is consistent with the early stages of research on plant genetic resources, in which morphological characterization and the establishment of collections provided the foundation for documenting and conserving genetic diversity. The subsequent period (2011–2019) showed convergence toward the central theme of *Chenopodium quinoa*, incorporating research lines associated with *genetics*, *protein*, *genotype*, *cultivation*, and *genetic differentiation*, indicating a transition toward studies aimed at understanding the genetic structure, nutritional composition, and agronomic adaptation of evaluated materials through advanced characterization tools. This evolution reflects the growing scientific interest in quinoa as a strategic crop because of its high nutritional value, broad environmental adaptability, and potential contribution to food security, promoting the incorporation of molecular and genetic tools into germplasm studies [(De Santis et al., 2016; Martín & Higuera, 2016; A. Shukla et al., 2018; Hammond Hammond et al., 2019; Romero et al., 2019; Salazar et al., 2019\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?eUU5hY).

The stabilization period (2020-2023) transformed accumulated knowledge into applications in plant breeding, highlighting the axis of *plant breeding* together with *germplasm*, *germplasm characterization*, and the geographical context of the Andes, demonstrating a stronger orientation toward the utilization of genetic diversity for the development of superior materials. The persistence of the term *Andes* reaffirms the importance of this region as one of the major centers of origin and diversification of native crops, where genetic richness continues to provide the basis for breeding programs [(Guilengue et al., 2020; Lazaridi et al., 2020; Cerón-Souza et al., 2021; Kroc et al., 2021; Laosatit et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2023\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?LOn4uY).The current period (2024-2026) demonstrates the consolidation of the research field around three dominant macrothemes: *germplasm*, *Chenopodium quinoa*, and *genetic diversity*, in which genetic, morphological, and plant breeding approaches converge, reflecting a trend toward integrated strategies for the conservation and utilization of genetic resources through molecular and phenotypic tools. This convergence demonstrates the increasing maturity of the research field, which is oriented toward integrating genomic, phenotypic, and agronomic information to optimize conservation, expand the utilization of genetic diversity, and strengthen the development of varieties adapted to climate change and sustainable agricultural scenarios  [(Akter et al., 2026; De la Cruz et al., 2025; Velasco et al., 2025; WEI et al., 2026\)](https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?skFBRM)

The thematic map reveals the intellectual structure of research by classifying clusters according to their degree of relevance (centrality) and development (density) (@fig-estructura%20). Motor themes exhibit a high level of development and importance within the scientific field, consolidating around agricultural production and optimization through terms such as *cultivation*, *plant breeding*, and *crop yield*, reflecting an increasing orientation toward the application of genetic knowledge to the development of materials with greater production potential. Basic themes constitute the fundamental core of the discipline, with high centrality but lower development, and are centered on *Chenopodium quinoa*, *germplasm*, and *genetic diversity*, demonstrating that the conservation and characterization of plant genetic resources remain essential pillars of research on Andean crops. Niche themes correspond to highly specialized research lines with lower overall interaction, focusing on *genetic differentiation*, *molecular analysis*, and *genetic analysis*, reflecting the incorporation of advanced tools to understand the genetic structure and relationships among populations (@fig-estructura%20). Conversely, emerging or declining themes exhibit lower centrality and density, encompassing general genetic studies associated with species such as *Solanum tuberosum* and *Oxalis tuberosa*, whereas intermediate nodes related to *genotype* and *genetic variability* indicate a transition toward research lines with greater applicability to plant breeding. The presence of *Amaranthus caudatus*, proteins, and wild populations reflects the continuity of studies aimed at understanding the biological diversity and functional attributes of Andean species of agricultural importance. This thematic distribution demonstrates an evolution from research focused on the conservation and characterization of genetic diversity toward approaches oriented toward the utilization of germplasm through molecular tools and plant breeding strategies, consistent with current trends in plant genetic resource research, where the integration of conservation, characterization, and sustainable utilization constitutes a key component for strengthening food security and crop adaptation to climate change.  

## ***The State of Germplasm Banks in Peru*** 

To identify the distribution of orphan crop germplasm collections in Peru, information was compiled on the institutions responsible for their conservation, their geographical location, the number of accessions recorded for each species, the conservation strategies employed, and the characterization status of the collections. In total, 16,904 accessions conserved in 11 institutions located across eight departments of the country were recorded: Cusco, Puno, Lima, Cajamarca, Junín, Amazonas, Ayacucho, and Arequipa (@fig-geografica). 

The department of Cusco concentrated the largest number of accessions, with 5,245 of the national total, distributed between the National University of San Antonio Abad of Cusco (UNSAAC) and the Andenes Agricultural Experimental Station (EEA-Andenes). The EEA-Andenes conserved 941 accessions of *Oxalis tuberosa*, 224 of *Tropaeolum tuberosum*, 192 of *Ullucus tuberosus*, and 20 varieties of *Chenopodium quinoa*, whereas UNSAAC recorded the largest collections in the department, with 1,600 accessions of *Amaranthus caudatus*, 1,500 and 1,200 of *Lupinus mutabilis*, 1,000 and 520 of *Chenopodium quinoa*, as well as 200 accessions of *Ullucus tuberosus*, 200 of *Oxalis tuberosa*, 100 of *Tropaeolum tuberosum*, 41 of *Smallanthus sonchifolius*, and 7 of *Arracacia xanthorrhiza*. The department of Puno ranked second, with 3,529 accessions conserved at the Illpa Agricultural Experimental Station (EEA-Illpa) and the National University of the Altiplano (UNA-Puno). The EEA-Illpa safeguarded 1,383 accessions of *Chenopodium quinoa* and 253 of *Chenopodium pallidicaule*, whereas UNA-Puno maintained 850 accessions of *Chenopodium quinoa*, 450 of *Lupinus mutabilis*, 350 of *Chenopodium pallidicaule*, 120 of *Oxalis tuberosa*, 60 of *Tropaeolum tuberosum*, 48 of *Ullucus tuberosus*, 10 of *Amaranthus caudatus*, and 5 of *Smallanthus sonchifolius*. In Lima, the International Potato Center (CIP) recorded 1,902 accessions, comprising 881 accessions of *Oxalis tuberosa*, 548 of *Ullucus tuberosus*, 216 of *Tropaeolum tuberosum*, 157 of *Lepidium meyenii*, 58 of *Smallanthus sonchifolius*, and 42 of *Arracacia xanthorrhiza* (@fig-geografica).

The high concentration of accessions in Cusco and Puno is consistent with the recognition of the central Andes as one of the major global centers of origin, domestication, and diversification of native crops, where interactions among altitudinal gradients, ecosystem diversity, and traditional agricultural practices have favored the conservation of substantial genetic variability. The considerable representation of Lima is primarily associated with the establishment of national and international institutions dedicated to the ex situ conservation, characterization, and distribution of plant genetic resources, rather than with the biogeographical characteristics of the department. This distribution demonstrates that the spatial organization of national collections depends on both ecological and cultural factors and the institutional capacity developed for germplasm collection, regeneration, and conservation. 

The departments of Cajamarca, Junín, Amazonas, Ayacucho, and Arequipa hosted smaller collections, although they represented an important diversity of conserved species. In Cajamarca, the Baños del Inca Agricultural Experimental Station recorded 602 accessions, comprising 388 of *Amaranthus caudatus* and 214 of *Smallanthus sonchifolius*. In Junín, the Santa Ana Agricultural Experimental Station conserved 436 accessions, corresponding to 235 of *Arracacia xanthorrhiza*, 180 of *Lupinus mutabilis*, and 21 of *Lepidium meyenii*. In Amazonas, the National University Toribio Rodríguez de Mendoza and the Amazonas Agricultural Experimental Station recorded 348 accessions, of which 311 corresponded to *Chenopodium quinoa*, 10 to *Tropaeolum tuberosum*, 10 to *Ullucus tuberosus*, 10 to *Oxalis tuberosa*, 5 to *Amaranthus caudatus*, and 2 to *Lupinus mutabilis*. The National University of San Cristóbal de Huamanga, in Ayacucho, conserved 270 accessions, comprising 250 of *Chenopodium quinoa*, 10 of *Chenopodium pallidicaule*, and 10 of *Lupinus mutabilis*, whereas the National University of San Agustín of Arequipa recorded 12 accessions, corresponding to 10 of *Chenopodium quinoa* and 2 of *Lupinus mutabilis* (@fig-geografica). Although these departments recorded fewer accessions, this does not necessarily imply lower genetic diversity. Previous studies have indicated that a substantial proportion of Andean agrobiodiversity continues to be conserved *in situ* by smallholder farmers and rural communities through the maintenance of locally adapted varieties under specific environmental conditions. The differences observed among departments may also reflect varying levels of institutional investment, intensity of collecting campaigns, and availability of infrastructure for *ex situ* conservation, rather than actual differences in the genetic richness of each region. 

Considering the national total, *Chenopodium quinoa* was the most represented species in germplasm banks, with 4,344 accessions, followed by *Amaranthus caudatus* (3,603), *Lupinus mutabilis* (3,344), *Oxalis tuberosa* (2,152), *Ullucus tuberosus* (998), *Chenopodium pallidicaule* (613), *Tropaeolum tuberosum* (610), *Smallanthus sonchifolius* (318), *Arracacia xanthorrhiza* (284), and *Lepidium meyenii* (178). The predominance of *Chenopodium quinoa*, *Amaranthus caudatus*, and *Lupinus mutabilis* is consistent with the increasing scientific and agronomic interest in these crops due to their high nutritional value, adaptation to marginal environments, and potential contribution to food security and resilience to climate change (@fig-geografica). Species such as *Lepidium meyenii*, *Arracacia xanthorrhiza*, and *Smallanthus sonchifolius* remain represented by fewer accessions, suggesting the need to strengthen national strategies for germplasm exploration, collection, and conservation to improve the representation of these plant genetic resources. The balanced conservation of all species of food importance constitutes a fundamental component for broadening the genetic base available for future breeding programs and ensuring the preservation of Peruvian agrobiodiversity. 

The conservation of orphan crop germplasm in Peru was carried out through three modalities: field, seed, and *in vitro* conservation, which were employed individually or in combination by the institutions evaluated (@tbl-estado-conservacion). Field conservation was the most frequent modality, being recorded in 10 of the 11 institutions, whereas seed conservation was implemented in eight institutions. *In vitro* conservation was recorded only at the International Potato Center (CIP), the Andenes Agricultural Experimental Station (EEA-Andenes), and the Baños del Inca Agricultural Experimental Station (EEA-BI), mainly for species such as *Oxalis tuberosa*, *Ullucus tuberosus*, *Tropaeolum tuberosum*, and *Smallanthus sonchifolius*. CIP was the only institution employing all three conservation modalities, whereas EEA-Andenes combined field and *in vitro* conservation (@tbl-estado-conservacion). The remaining institutions conserved their collections using one or two modalities, depending on the species maintained. 

The implementation of multiple conservation modalities is consistent with international recommendations for germplasm bank management, which indicate that the selection of conservation methods should consider the biological characteristics of the species and their propagation mechanisms. Seed conservation constitutes an efficient strategy for species with orthodox seeds, whereas field and *in vitro* conservation are essential for vegetatively propagated species or those with limitations for conventional storage. Combining these modalities increases the security of collections and reduces the risk of loss of conserved genetic material 

Phenotypic characterization was the predominant methodology and was implemented in most of the collections evaluated. Genomic characterization was reported at the International Potato Center, the National University Toribio Rodríguez de Mendoza, the National University of San Cristóbal de Huamanga, and the National University of San Agustín of Arequipa, whereas biochemical characterization was reported at the International Potato Center, the National University of the Altiplano, and the National University Toribio Rodríguez de Mendoza. The International Potato Center was the only institution that integrated phenotypic, genomic, and biochemical approaches within the same collection, whereas the remaining institutions relied primarily on morphological and agronomic assessments, complemented by genomic or biochemical analyses for specific species.

Morphological and agronomic assessment remains the principal approach used in germplasm banks because of its importance for describing phenotypic attributes and identifying variation of potential agronomic value. The incorporation of genomic and biochemical tools expands the scientific and applied value of collections by enabling the identification of genetic variants and compounds of interest for breeding programs and the development of crops with greater adaptive capacity and nutritional value. The integration of these complementary characterization approaches constitutes a strategic framework for maximizing the utilization of conserved plant genetic resources and strengthening their application in agricultural research and development.

**Note.** Information collected through institutional surveys and supplemented with official records from the germplasm banks of the National Institute of Agrarian Innovation (INIA).  

## ***Challenges for Conservation***

Insufficient financial resources constitute one of the main limitations to the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources, particularly for collections of orphan and underutilized crops (@fig-limitaciones). Germplasm banks require sustained investment in the storage, periodic regeneration, morphological and molecular characterization, accession documentation, and maintenance of specialized infrastructure. Budgetary constraints have been recognized as a recurrent challenge in national and international conservation programs, affecting institutional capacity to ensure the long-term conservation and effective access to germplasm. Inadequate infrastructure increases the vulnerability of biological collections, while the loss of genetic diversity limits opportunities for developing materials adapted to emerging production and climatic scenarios. 

Institutional willingness to exchange germplasm represents a fundamental element for strengthening national and international networks for the conservation and utilization of plant genetic resources. The exchange of genetic material facilitates scientific research, breeding programs, and the expansion of the genetic base available for species with agronomic and nutritional potential. Modern germplasm banks play a central role in the safe and regulated mobilization of plant genetic resources, promoting cooperation among institutions and access to materials of interest for sustainable agriculture. The high level of willingness reported by the participating institutions highlights opportunities to consolidate collaborative mechanisms aimed at the characterization, regeneration, and conservation of existing collections. Strengthening the technical and financial capacities of germplasm banks is therefore essential to maximize the utilization of conserved material and ensure its availability for future generations and for agricultural research and development programs. 

## ***Limitations and perspectives***

This study provides a comprehensive overview of the state of scientific research and germplasm banks for orphan crops in Peru, although several limitations should be acknowledged. The bibliometric analysis was based exclusively on the Scopus database; therefore, publications indexed in other bibliographic sources were not included. Information on germplasm banks was collected from the main institutions responsible for the conservation of plant genetic resources in the country; however, other entities may maintain orphan crop collections whose information was not documented or made available during the study period. It was not possible to determine the extent of duplication among conserved collections because of the lack of standardized information and an integrated national database capable of comparing accessions maintained by different institutions.

This study constitutes the first national assessment to integrate information on scientific production and the main germplasm collections of orphan crops in Peru, establishing a baseline for future initiatives aimed at expanding the national inventory, strengthening collection documentation, and promoting greater integration among institutions involved in the conservation of plant genetic resources. The implementation of a national platform for information exchange among germplasm banks, complemented by molecular characterization of the collections, would facilitate the identification of duplicate accessions, optimization of storage capacity, and more efficient allocation of conservation resources. Coordinating these efforts would accelerate the identification of genotypes with promising agronomic traits and strengthen the conservation, management, and utilization of plant genetic resources for food and agriculture in Peru.

# **CONCLUSIONS**

The bibliometric analysis revealed sustained growth in research on orphan crops of relevance to Peru, with *Chenopodium quinoa* emerging as the central focus of scientific production, followed by species such as *Amaranthus caudatus*, *Lupinus mutabilis*, and *Chenopodium pallidicaule*. The thematic evolution showed a transition from studies focused on morphological characterization and germplasm conservation toward research addressing genetic diversity, plant breeding, and the integration of molecular tools, reflecting the increasing importance of these crops for food security, climate change adaptation, and sustainable agriculture.

The survey conducted among institutions responsible for germplasm conservation showed that Peruvian germplasm banks maintain a broad diversity of plant genetic resources, concentrated mainly in Cusco, Puno, and Lima, where institutions such as UNSAAC, INIA, and CIP play strategic roles in ex situ conservation. However, the assessment revealed differences in management capacity, infrastructure, and documentation among institutions, as well as the need to strengthen characterization, regeneration, digitization, and germplasm exchange. These findings provide a baseline for guiding national strategies aimed at strengthening the conservation and sustainable utilization of plant genetic resources from Andean crops with current and potential importance for Peruvian agriculture.
